title: Borrowed Roots
summary: Foundries kept rebuilds legal enough to work by moving one surviving machine's record through many frames; the Authority calls that continuity counterfeit.
body: A root began as a collar number, a set of test marks and a place in the Compact ledger. During the Foundry Winter, damaged machines outlasted all three. Shops shifted serviceable limbs, reactors and cockpits into whatever frame could still walk, then copied the least-disputed number across the result.

The exchange was not a command channel. It was an agreement between yards: one relay carried the borrowed record, one quarry cut a matching plate and one clerk wrote the repair as continuity rather than construction. One borrowed serial could cover several surviving roots, with haulers and pumps carried under the same service account. The yards multiplied records, not roots.

The Recall Authority reads each copy as a false claim against state property. The foundries read it as the paper bridge that kept their settlements alive. By the time a custody tender reaches the original collar, six machines may be carrying copies of its number, and six families may depend on which claim the warrant accepts. Each walker still needs its own surviving physical root.
